t: Among seven people A, B, C, D, E, F and G, scored different marks (out of 100) in an exam. A scored the highest. G's marks were a multiple of 9, but more than 85. Nobody scored more than 92. The sum of the marks of G and F was 150. D scored more than only E. C scored more than F and less than B. E scored 33 marks. Which of the following can be a possible score for D?
e: G's marks are a multiple of 9, greater than 85, and since nobody scores more than 92 (and A is the highest, so A > G), G must be 90 (the only multiple of 9 between 85 and 92). So F = 150 - 90 = 60. The ranking order becomes: A > G > B > C > F > D > E. Since E = 33 and F = 60, and D scored more than only E (D is placed between F and E), D must satisfy 33 < D < 60. Checking options: only 48 fits this range. Answer: 48.

t: K, L, M, W, X, Y and Z scored different marks in an exam. K scored more than only three people. Y scored less than only L and M. W scored more than Z but less than X. L did not score the highest marks. How many people scored less than X?
e: K scored more than exactly 3 people, so K is 4th (3 above, 3 below) in a group of 7. Y is below only L and M, so top-to-bottom starts with L and M (in some order) then Y. Since L is not the highest, M must be highest: M > L > Y. Since K is 4th and 3 people are already above K (M, L, Y), the order so far is M > L > Y > K. The remaining three — X, W, Z — go below K, with W > Z and W W > Z. Full order: M > L > Y > K > X > W > Z. People scoring less than X: W and Z = 2 people.

X < Y trivially true ✓. This full order satisfies all conditions. Since Y is the highest, nobody scored more than Y. Answer: None.

t: K, L, M, W, X, Y and Z scored different marks in an exam. K scored more than both L and W but less than Y. X scored less than only Y. Neither L nor M scored the lowest marks. Z scored more than L but less than M. K scored more than M. Who scored the third-lowest marks?
e: X is below only Y, so order starts Y > X. K X > K so far. We're told K > M > Z > L (chain). Also K > W. Since neither L nor M is lowest, W must be the lowest (as W is not otherwise constrained upward). Full order: Y > X > K > M > Z > L > W. Counting from the bottom: W = lowest (1st lowest), L = 2nd lowest, Z = 3rd lowest. Answer: Z.

t: Seven students H, I, J, K, L, M and N have all scored a unique number of marks. H scored only more than N. Marks of three students were between the marks of J and I. I did not score the highest marks. How many students scored less than J?
e: H scored more than only N, so H is 2nd lowest and N is lowest. Three students lie between J and I in rank. Since I is not the highest, J must be the highest — if J is at position 1, three students fill positions 2-4, then I is at position 5, and the remaining two lowest positions (6, 7) go to H and N (H above N). This fits all conditions perfectly. Since J is the highest scorer, every other one of the 6 remaining students scored less than J. Answer: 6.

t: Seven students of a school, E, F, G, H, I, J, and K have all obtained different scores. E's score was less than only one student. K scored more than only one person. One arrangement satisfying everything: F > E > G > H > I > K > J. This confirms J has the least score.

t: Seven people K, B, M, C, R, P, and S have different heights. C is taller than K. B is shorter than M. P is shorter than M and B. C is not taller than P. S is not taller than K. M is shorter than only one person. Who is the shortest?

t: Seven teachers M, N, O, P, Q, R and S take different number of tuitions. P takes more tuitions than S. M takes more tuitions than Q. R takes the second highest number of tuitions. The number of tuitions that O takes is less than only that of four teachers. N takes less tuitions than P but more than M. Q takes the least number of tuitions. S takes the second lowest number of tuitions. In terms of the number of tuitions taken, who is between N and S?
e: Q is lowest (position 7), S is 2nd lowest (position 6), R is 2nd highest (position 2), O is 5th (exactly 4 teachers take more than O, out of 7, so O has 4 above, 2 below). This fixes positions: R=2, O=5, S=6, Q=7. Remaining positions 1, 3, 4 go to P, N, M, with N M, giving P > N > M. Assign P=1, N=3, M=4. Full order (most to least tuitions): P > R > N > M > O > S > Q. Between N (position 3) and S (position 6) lie positions 4 and 5, which are M and O. Answer: M, O.

t: Amit's father is aged five times more than Amit. After 6 years, he would be three and a half times of Amit's age. After further 9 years, how many times of Amit's age would he be?

After 6 yrs (6+6=12, 36+6=42): ratio 42/12=3.5 ✓ (matches). After further 9 yrs (total 15 yrs from now): Amit=6+15=21, father=36+15=51. Ratio=51/21 = 17/7 = 2(3/7) times.

t: In a class 220 students appeared in an examination. The rank of Rahul in the list of passed students is 145 th from top and 51 st from bottom. How many students failed in an examination?

e: When A takes n more days than the time taken by both A and B and B takes m more days than the time taken by both A and B together to complete the same piece of work, then the number of days in which A and B both together will complete the same piece of work = √(n x m) Here n = 6 and m = 24 Required number of days = √(6 x 24) = √144 = 12 days
